*Speaking as the farmer:*

Aiya, I've been doing this for 35 years so I mostly just do what I've always done. My old man and me, we're the only ones left on the farm — kids went to the city long ago. So whatever we plant, we have to be able to manage ourselves, or pay someone from the village to help out.

I've got about 10 mu. Three mu of it is my cotton patch — been cotton ground for years, the soil's right for it. The other seven mu or so I do wheat then maize, same as most folks around here. That way even if the maize gets hit by bad weather, we still got wheat in the grain bin for flour, and the other way around too.

**Wheat** — I plant around Cold Dew time (寒露, mid-October), after the maize comes off. I buy one bag of compound fertilizer (复合肥) per mu before planting, that's about 40 kg, and another half-bag of urea when it starts getting tall in spring. My neighbor lady across the path does about the same. I water it maybe three times — once before winter, once when it's greening up, once when it's filling the grain. Water costs money at the well so I don't do it unless I have to. If I get 400 kg a mu I'm happy, my man's happy.

**Maize** — Right after wheat harvest in June, no time to waste. I hire the village fellow with the planter, costs me some yuan but at my age I can't be bending over planting by hand anymore. One bag of compound at planting, maybe a little urea when it's knee-high if it looks yellow. Usually only need to water once or twice, the summer rain does most of the work.

**Cotton** — Plant end of April when the ground's warm. Cotton's the hardest — picking takes forever and my back's not what it was. I'll hire two village women for a few days during each picking. I use less fertilizer on cotton than my neighbor, I can't afford to put a lot down. Spray for bollworm when I see them chewing. Prices for cotton aren't great these last years but I've always done it, don't want to change now.

I'm careful with money. If I spend too much on fertilizer and the price of grain drops, we eat into our savings. Better to put a little less and take what comes.
